canberra.title: New court will focus on workplace justice
canberra.snippet: A new Fair Work Court is being established to streamline workplace dispute resolutions and provide what the Federal Government says will ...
canberra.content:
The Federal Government is creating a new Fair Work Court to work alongside the Fair Work Commission to streamline workplace disputes. Photo; File

A new Fair Work Court is being established to streamline workplace dispute resolutions and provide what the Federal Government says will be simpler, fairer and faster justice for working Australians.

But the Business Council of Australia has cautioned that it shouldn’t be seen as a substitute for fixing the complexity the government has itself created in workplace laws.

The new federal body will provide a specialist forum for resolving workplace relations disputes, employing specialist judges with workplace relations expertise to sit on the court.

The aim is that these judges will support faster, simpler and more accessible dispute resolution.

Anthony Albanese delivered the news during his speech to the Labor Party National Conference on Thursday (23 July), saying it will be led by judges who will work “seamlessly” with the Fair Work Commission.

“Australians who have been underpaid hundreds, even thousands, of dollars shouldn’t have to wait years for justice, or be told their case will cost more than their claim,” Mr Albanese said.

“That’s why Labor will fix it – with the Fair Work Court to resolve disputes faster and at lower cost, benefiting employees and employers alike.”

The current court system for workers and employers can be costly and complex to navigate, with slow response rates.

Some workers and small businesses are spending more than two years fighting for a resolution that the PM says should be simple.

The government will now consult on the design of the proposed court this year.

That consultation will help shape how the court works, including how it will operate alongside the FWC, and how it will improve the navigation of disputes.

Workers, employers, and legal experts will be able to provide feedback before the government considers the court’s final design and next steps.

Details of the consultation process will be released soon.

BCA chief executive Bran Black said instead of adding another layer of red tape with the new court, the government should make the system simpler to understand for both employees and employers.

“For a small business, a case that costs more than it’s worth is not only unfair, it can be the difference between staying open or closing its doors,” he said.

“We support faster, simpler and more affordable workplace resolutions. But this announcement has the potential to yet again add another layer of process without any real practical benefit.

“This complexity is also taking workplaces back to the old days of more combative disputes, rather than encouraging the cooperative workplaces for which we should be striving.

“If this court proceeds, judges must be appointed on merit, independent and impartial so that both workers and employers can trust that it is fair.”

The Prime Minister also announced that young workers aged 18 to 20 will soon be paid as adults and no longer receive junior award rates as is currently the case.

“After decades of union campaigning – and remember back at my first conference in 1986, speaking about youth wages – workers aged 18, 19, and 20 are finally being paid like the adults that they are,” he said.

Workers aged 18 to 20 are currently paid less than older employees doing the same jobs.

canberra.title: Stephen-Smith set to replace Berry as Deputy Chief Minister
canberra.snippet: Rachel Stephen-Smith is expected to be elected unopposed as the ACT’s new Deputy Chief Minister when the Labor caucus meets on Mond...
canberra.content:
Senior minister Rachel-Stephen-Smith is understood to be the sole nominee for ACT Deputy Chief Minister. Photo: ACT Government.

Rachel Stephen-Smith is expected to be elected unopposed as the ACT’s new Deputy Chief Minister when the Labor caucus meets on Monday (27 July).

Sources said the senior minister was the obvious choice for the role, and that she is in the same Left faction as her predecessor, Yvette Berry.

Ms Berry resigned from cabinet on Thursday (23 July) after the tabling of the ACT Integrity Commission report on Operation Kingfisher.

The investigation into the Campbell Primary School modernisation project tender process did not find any wrongdoing by Ms Berry, but the conduct of her former chief of staff, Joshua Ceramidas and the former director-general of the Education Directorate, Katy Haire, was found to be seriously corrupt.

They were found to have favoured a union-preferred contractor over the more highly ranked rival, costing taxpayers an extra $1 million.

Sources said Ms Stephen-Smith had earned the right to be Chief Minister Andrew Barr’s Deputy and was well liked and respected by members across factions and by stakeholders.

“She’s a senior minister in cabinet, she’s done a lot of hard work … she’s just the natural next pick,” one source said.

Another said it would be strange to have two people in the same faction as leader and deputy, but the 2028 election and Mr Barr’s political future would also be a consideration.

“Surely that’s in people’s minds, that they want to make sure that the strongest person goes into the deputy [role],” they said.

“I can’t see a world in which it is not Rachel Stephen-Smith.”

Treasurer Chris Steel was thought to be in the mix, but he is from the Right faction and still carrying baggage from the $77 million failed payroll system project and the MyWay + ticketing debacle.

There did not appear to be any factional manoeuvring or battles around Monday’s caucus meeting, which will also vote for a new minister, expected to be the Right’s Caitlin Tough from the southern seat of Brindabella.

Sources said she was ready to step up and in a faction, while her Brindabella colleague Taimus Werner-Gibbings was unaligned.

On the redistribution of portfolios, which Mr Barr said would not be radical, one source thought Michael Pettersson – already Skills, Training and Industrial Relations Minister – could pick up education and housing.

Housing would be a natural fit for Planning Minister Steel, but he already had a lot on his plate as Treasurer and Transport Minister.

The only hiccup could be Mr Pettersson’s membership of the CFMEU, which was named in the Commission’s report.

His lesser portfolios – Business, Arts and Creative Industries; Children, Youth and Families; and Multicultural Affairs – were considered suited to a newcomer like Ms Tough finding their feet.

One source said that if Mr Barr chose to call it a day, Ms Stephen-Smith would be the best replacement if Labor were returned in 2028.

But the one to watch for deputy would be Attorney-General Tara Cheyne.

She had the smarts, and could be the dark horse to upset the view that Mr Steel, also in the Right faction, would be deputy.

Questions to Ms Stephen-Smith, Mr Steel and Ms Cheyne about whether they would be putting their hand up only brought a response from the Chief Minister’s office.

“The Chief Minister will make an announcement on the new Ministry, including the new Deputy Chief Minister, after the caucus meeting,” a spokesperson said.

canberra.title: ‘Acute breach of trust’: Stepfather has no remorse for assault that broke four-year-old boy’s skull
canberra.snippet: CONTENT WARNING: This article contains references to family violence and details that may distress some readers. The “light has gon...
canberra.content:
The four-year-old child called the offender ‘pa’ or ‘dad’. Photo: Michelle Kroll.

CONTENT WARNING: This article contains references to family violence and details that may distress some readers.

The “light has gone out” of a four-year-old child in the aftermath of an assault that left him with a skull fracture, a court has heard.

The fracture, along with other serious injuries, was sustained in September 2023 at a time when he was with his stepfather.

The man, whom Region is unable to name for legal reasons, did not visibly react when he heard he would be sent to prison during sentencing in the ACT Supreme Court on Friday (24 July).

Justice Belinda Baker described the offending as being an “acute breach of trust” that occurred when the boy’s mother “left the victim in the care of the offender”.

She said the injuries occurred during a two-hour window, when the offender’s then-partner left for an appointment, and the child was alone with the man.

“Call records show that at around 1:43 pm, the offender tried to call the victim’s mother twice … [He also made] several Google searches about ‘child head injuries’,” she said.

Later that day, a mechanic remembered seeing the victim vomiting water. Paramedics were called to the family’s home at around 3:30 pm.

The child was taken to hospital, where he was found to have suffered a head fracture, brain bruising, a brain bleed and three hairline rib fractures.

Justice Baker said a paediatrician who examined the victim also found 34 bruises on the boy’s body that were judged to be “not consistent with normal rough and tumble play”.

It’s still unclear how the injuries occurred.

The man claimed that the child fell from his bike onto concrete outside the apartment, but Justice Baker rejected this claim.

She said it was “unlikely that the injuries can be explained by a fall from a bicycle”, pointing to two doctors’ reports into the victim’s injuries.

“Those reports stated that the quality, distribution, character and clustering are highly suggestive of inflicted injuries and more likely represented inflicted blunt force trauma,” Justice Baker said.

She said that during an interview with police, the boy said that he had been “‘naughty'” and that “dad made his head hurt”.

However, she also rejected the prosecution’s submission that the injuries were caused by the man using an instrument to strike the child, saying she couldn’t conclude that “simply from the nature of the injuries sustained”.

Justice Baker found that, regardless, the injuries were caused by force “not of a minimal nature and that the victim sustained his injuries as a result of the application of force”.

“I am unable to make any findings [in the] way of aggravation or motivation, as to the way the force was applied,” she said.

During sentencing, the court heard details of how the boy’s injuries, as well as his trauma from the assault, continue to impact him and his family.

In a victim impact statement, one relative outlined how the offending has changed the previously “happy, outgoing, curious, adventurous” child’s personality.

“It is as if a light has gone out – he is no longer the child he was … He refuses to sleep alone and still constantly wakes up to check that I am still with him,” the relative outlined.

“‘He is scared of the dark and terrified of strangers.”

Justice Baker also found the man had shown no remorse for his offending, having told a court report’s author that while it “may look bad” in court, he denied inflicting the injuries.

The man was also on parole at the time of the offending and had a criminal history in NSW and the ACT that included property damage, assault and other offences.

She said those factors meant “significant weight” in sentencing needed to be awarded to specific deterrence.

For a charge of aggravated assault causing actual bodily harm, the man was handed a sentence of imprisonment of two-and-a-half years.

He has an 18-month non-parole period, which will end in January 2028.

If this story has raised any concerns for you, 1800RESPECT, the national 24-hour sexual assault, family and domestic violence counselling line, can be contacted on 1800 737 732. Help and support are also available through the Canberra Rape Crisis Centre on 02 6247 2525, the Domestic Violence Crisis Service ACT on 02 6280 0900, the Sexual Violence Legal Services on 6257 4377 and Lifeline on 13 11 14. In an emergency, call Triple Zero.

canberra.title: US hits Australia with slave labour tariffs
canberra.snippet: Almost all Australian exports to the United States will be hit with a 12.5 per cent tariff for what the Trump administration describes as...
canberra.content:
US Trade Representative Jamieson Greer says Australia has failed to impose and enforce prohibitions against slave labour. Photo: US Government.

Almost all Australian exports to the United States will be hit with a 12.5 per cent tariff for what the Trump administration describes as a “failure to impose and effectively enforce a prohibition on the importation of goods produced with forced labour”.

The US Trade Department has issued a statement confirming the immediate start to the previously threatened tariffs, which Australia is criticising as completely unjustified.

Australia is one of 54 countries targeted with the new punitive 12.5 per cent tariff.

The list includes New Zealand, the United Kingdom, China, Brazil, Egypt, India, Israel, Japan, Singapore, Russia and Norway.

Bizarrely, some other economies such as the European Union, Canada and Mexico are attracting a lesser 10 per cent tariff because the US says they have imposed slave labour prohibitions but simply failed to enforce them.

All up, 60 international economies will be hit with the US’s slave labour tariffs.

“Today, Ambassador Jamieson Greer is taking final action, at President Trump’s direction, under Section 301 of the Trade Act of 1974 by imposing tariffs on 60 economies for their failure to impose and effectively enforce a prohibition on the importation of goods produced with forced labour,” the US Trade Department’s statement said.

“Today’s action comes after the Office of the United States Trade Representative’s (USTR) investigations, which included two rounds of public hearings, more than 2100 public comments, and engagement with our trading partners to remedy these longstanding concerns.

“President Trump recognises that decades of moral suasion have not eradicated forced labour from global supply chains,” US Trade Representative Jamieson Greer said in a statement overnight on Friday (24 July) AEST.

“The United States has had a forced labour import ban for nearly a century, and rigorously enforces it; it’s well past time for our trading partners to do the same.

“Today’s action will begin to correct what is both a human rights abuse and a distortive trade practice to improve the welfare of workers everywhere.

“I am encouraged by the trading partners who have moved quickly to adopt forced labour import prohibitions, and look forward to ensuring their effective enforcement.”

Australia is pushing back. The Federal Government is saying this country does not deserve a tariff over slave labour as Australia has world-leading laws against modern slavery.

Deputy Prime Minister Richard Marles said the government was vigorously stating its anti-slave labour credentials to the US.

“We share an objective there to stamp that out,” Mr Marles said.

“But we would have also made clear that the legal regime that we have in Australia in respect of forced labour is amongst the best legal regimes that exist in the world today.

“And we’re making that point very clearly to the Trump administration as well … This, in our view, makes no sense.”

Trade Minister Don Farrell has also commented on the development, calling the tariffs “completely unjustified”.

Speaking from Labor’s national conference in Adelaide on Friday, the minister said the government was serious in its efforts to oppose modern slavery.

“We continue to maintain that these tariffs are unjustified. Australia is a country that deals with the issue of modern slavery seriously,” Senator Farrell said.

“And from my point of view, the government’s point of view, we will continue to argue very strongly for the removal of these tariffs.”

The Australian Chamber of Commerce and Industry (ACCI) has also condemned the new tariffs, saying their imposition ignores a free trade agreement (FTA) the US has had with Australia for more than 20 years.

ACCI chief executive officer Andrew McKellar described the decision as “ludicrous and unjustified” and said the business chamber wants to work with the Federal Government to help resolve the issue.

“The US has again unilaterally cast aside its FTA obligations with Australia,” Mr McKellar said.

“Australia and the United States signed a free trade agreement in 2005 for the purposes of enhancing trade, and these tariffs are in clear breach of that agreement.

“What makes it even more unjustified is the fact the US is imposing these tariffs on the basis of forced labour or modern slavery.

“Australia has some of the highest protections and enforcement against modern slavery anywhere in the world.

“The US administration’s decision will reduce trade and increase costs for US businesses and consumers.”

Labor recently moved to beef up its anti-slavery laws in the face of the US tariffs threat.

The government announced new legislation will soon be drafted seeking to apply the Criminal Code to Australian companies with an annual consolidated revenue of more than $100 million, and that can’t prove they have tried to stop worker exploitation in the goods they are selling.

canberra.title: ‘Enough to kill you’: Alleged drunk driver more than eight times over legal limit
canberra.snippet: A Holt woman has claimed that she just drank a bottle of red wine before allegedly crashing her car and recording a breath test result of...
canberra.content:
The court heard the woman claimed to have only drunk one bottle of wine before the alleged offending. Photo: Michelle Kroll.

A Holt woman has claimed that she just drank a bottle of red wine before allegedly crashing her car and recording a breath test result of 0.416.

Agot Deng Aleer, 36, briefly faced the ACT Magistrates Court on Friday (24 July), when she was charged with multiple traffic offences.

Earlier today, an ACT Policing spokesperson alleged that between 5 pm and 7:30 pm yesterday (23 July), police received multiple reports of a grey Kia Sorento driving erratically on Wattle Street and Ginninderra Drive in Lyneham.

“The vehicle was allegedly driving onto gutters, swerving across lanes, rapidly accelerating and decelerating, and on one occasion reversed into a parked vehicle,” they said.

At about 8 pm, police allegedly found the Kia Sorento reversing out of a driveway in Macgregor.

Officers approached the vehicle and allegedly saw the woman in the driver’s seat while three young children were also in the car.

“Police believe the three children were in the vehicle during the whole incident,” the police spokesperson said.

The woman was arrested for breaching her bail conditions, with an alcohol breath screening test allegedly returning a positive result.

She was taken to Belconnen Police Station, where she allegedly returned a breath analysis result of 0.416, more than eight times the legal alcohol limit.

In court, Aleer’s defence lawyer said her client had no reported criminal history and described her caring responsibilities for her three young children as being a protective factor.

She also proposed “quite strict” conditions that would bar Aleer from drinking and include breath testing, alongside an existing bail condition not to drive.

“[Aleer] has not yet had the benefit of several conditions – including conditions of supervision and monitoring by the court’s alcohol and drugs service,” the lawyer said of Aleer’s bail for separate alleged offending.

The prosecutor called for bail to be refused, describing Aleer as having allegedly been “extremely intoxicated”.

“The driving only ceased due to an accident,” she alleged.

She also said the alleged offending occurred at a “time of day when you can still expect a large number of road users” to be on the roads.

The prosecutor also said the alleged bail breach indicated that Aleer “cannot comply” with further court orders if released on conditional liberty.

Ultimately, Magistrate James Stewart refused bail, speaking to the woman directly about her claim she drank one red wine bottle before the alleged offending.

“Must have been a whopper of a bottle,” he told her.

Magistrate Stewart said that the allegations raised “an extreme risk” to the community, while the fresh offending appeared to represent “receptive and extreme” alleged drink driving by the woman.

“[Your alleged blood alcohol level was] 0.416. People die at 0.416 … That’s enough to kill you – do you understand that?”

Aleer is facing charges of driving a motor vehicle with alcohol in breath, driving while a licence is suspended, driving under the influence of liquor, not giving particulars to the owner of property damaged in a crash and breaching her bail conditions.

She will next return to court on a future date. No pleas were entered.

The police spokesperson asks that anyone who has dashcam footage of a grey Kia Sorento with ACT registration YRO00N from between 5 pm and 7:30 pm yesterday come forward.

Anyone who can assist police with the alleged offending should provide their contact details to Crime Stoppers ACT, quoting 8451600.

australia.title: University courses covering Israel-Palestine should be audited, Julian Leeser tells royal commission
australia.snippet: Inquiry’s focus this week is on security for the Jewish community, with the MP telling the commissioner his son is afraid to attend synag...
australia.content:
The shadow education minister, Julian Leeser, has called for universities to undertake an audit of any classes that teach about the Jewish community, Israel or Palestine.

Appearing before the royal commission into antisemitism and social cohesion on Friday, Leeser said he had been “very concerned” about antisemitism on university campuses and was not satisfied with how vice-chancellors had addressed the issue after the 7 October 2023 Hamas terrorist attack.

“I’ve been particularly unhappy with the responses that I’ve received [from vice-chancellors] in relation to their failure to … audit courses dealing with the Israel-Palestine conflict to ensure that both sides are presented in the best way possible so that students are best prepared to make their own mind up,” he said.

This week, the inquiry focused on security for the Jewish community, hearing a broad consensus that the risk had risen post 7 October.

Leeser put a series of recommendations to the commissioner, including for the government to legislate that all universities adopt the International Holocaust Remembrance Alliance (IHRA) definition of antisemitism, instead of their own definitions, as the federal government recently mandated. The IHRA definition is contentious because of concerns it could be used to shut down criticism of Israel.

Last year, the chief executive of the Group of Eight, Vicki Thomson, said members had advised that the IHRA definition was “not workable” in an Australian context as it may limit academic freedom.

Leeser said all universities should also undertake “an audit of what’s being taught about Jews and Israel in their classrooms” and remove any “antisemitic materials”. He said universities that taught about the Israel-Palestine conflict should make sure their course materials came from “credible sources” that were “balanced”.

Asked how to ensure classroom content was “balanced”, he said people believed they had shown both sides if they had a Palestinian and Israeli perspective, “but one of those perspectives is a full-throated defence by advocates” and “the other perspective is not at all”.

Last week, the inquiry heard from vice-chancellors of Australia’s largest universities who said they had sharply changed their protest policies since 2023, prompting warnings of restricted academic freedom.

Leeser said antisemitism was apparent in “three main vectors” today: “the far right among neo-Nazis, among radical Islamists, and among the academic and cultural left”.

The Dor Foundation’s inaugural CEO Tahli Blicblau agreed that “Islamic extremism” and the “extreme-far right” were the most dangerous radical ideologies perpetuating antisemitism, but also took aim at “fringe elements of the far-left and conspiracy movements”. The foundation was launched to combat antisemitism last year.

She said the pro-Palestine movement may have some similar ideological drivers as the “radical far left threat” but “the vast majority” of pro-Palestine protesters weren’t motivated by violence towards Jewish people.

Blicblau said in an “unprecedented” environment of elevated security risk towards the Jewish community following the Bondi terror attack, greater integration was needed between New South Wales law enforcement and Jewish groups.

“If you accept the level of threat is severe … then it follows that the level of integration and engagement between the Jewish community and the law enforcement and intelligence agencies needs to be sufficiently mature to meet the scale of the threat,” she said.

Leeser also gave emotional evidence of his experience on 14 December 2025, the day of Bondi terror attack, when he was attending a Hanukkah event in northern Sydney at the time news broke of the fatal shootings. He said his seven-year-old son “cried inconsolably” and asked him “Dad, are we going to be safe?”

Leeser said since then, his son had been afraid to attend synagogues and outdoor communal events.

“What sort of Australia are we setting up that a seven-year-old child doesn’t feel safe going to a place of worship?” he said. “That’s not the Australia I know and love and it’s not the Australia I want for my children or anyone’s children.”

australia.title: Julian Leeser says his son no longer feels safe at Jewish events – as it happened
australia.snippet: This blog is now closed Get our breaking news email , free app or daily news podcast Australian exports sent to the US will be hit with a...
australia.content:
Julian Leeser tells royal commission his son no longer feels safe at Jewish events

Caitlin Cassidy

Back to the antisemitism royal commission, where the Liberal MP Julian Leeser has been giving evidence.

Leeser has recalled his own experience on 14 December, the day of the terror attack in Bondi.

He was attending an outdoor Hanukkah event in northern Sydney at the time.

Holding back tears, he says he remembers his son’s fear when the news broke.

Leeser had made a speech at the event saying he “recognised that it had been a tough year for the Jewish community, but hoped that things would be better”, when a rabbi pulled him aside and said 50 shots had been fired at Bondi.

He told the rabbi they should get down as quickly as possible, because they didn’t know if what had happened at Bondi was more coordinated, and that:

When I came down , it was apparent that people had been killed in the events at Bondi … By that time there were lots of adults who were sharing pictures … And they’re in disbelief.

My son at that time was seven and my daughter was three. And my son had overheard the adults talking about the fact that people had been shot and killed in Bondi. And he cried inconsolably … He sat with his legs crossed saying, ‘Dad, are we going to be safe?’.

This has affected him deeply.

Leeser said he couldn’t guarantee to his son that they would be safe. Since then, he has been afraid to attend synagogues and outdoor communal events.

What sort of Australia are we setting up that a seven-year-old child doesn’t feel safe going to a place of worship?

That’s not the Australia I know and love and it’s not the Australia I want for my children or anyone’s children.

    Welcome

What we learned – Friday 24 July

That’s all for our live coverage today.

Before we go, let’s recap the day’s top headlines:

  • Jim Chalmers has claimed rightwing political parties will “prey on” voter insecurities about a worsening economy while championing “anti-worker” policies.

  • Australia’s resilient labour market continues to be a bright spot in the nation’s economy.

  • The world’s longest-range commercial aircraft has been greeted by plane-spotters and aviation enthusiasts after arriving in Melbourne on Friday morning.

  • The prime minister has spoken to his new UK counterpart, Andy Burnham, who was sworn in on Monday, congratulating him on his appointment and invited him to visit Australia.

  • Australian exports sent to the US will be hit with a 12.5% tariff as the US president imposes levies on more than 80 nations.

  • The ABC 0mbudsman is reviewing two episodes of Four Corners by former reporter Mahmood Fazal following concerns about the veracity of sources.

  • Australia’s peak medicines regulator has issued product warnings for several type 2 diabetes and obesity-related drugs over the potential to cause a “rare but severe” form of eye disorder.

  • The entire Queensland police pistol arsenal – more than 14,000 weapons – will be replaced by new guns.

  • Socceroos star Cristian Volpato has allegedly tested positive for cocaine, after police stopped him speeding over a harbour bridge.

  • Liberal MP Julian Leeser tells royal commission his son no longer feels safe at Jewish events.

  • Trade minister Don Farrell has described the Trump administration’s decision to impose a 12.5% tariff on Australian exports because Australia is not doing enough to combat forced labour as “crazy”.

Thanks for joining us and have a lovely weekend!

Conference fight looms on Husic’s Israel resolution

Dan Jervis-Bardy

As we reported earlier, Ed Husic is fighting internal resistance as he attempts to pass a resolution at Labor’s national conference condemning Israel’s war in Gaza and urging the government to withdraw officials from Australia’s embassy in Tel Aviv.

The Maritime Union of Australia has agreed to second Husic’s proposal, meaning it’s a step closer to being debated on the conference floor on Saturday.

The government has been working to avoid a debate on Israel and Palestine overshadowing the conference, which has been carefully stage-managed to avoid public conflicts.

Guardian Australia understands Husic’s resolution has several elements, including one clause recognising the 2024 decision of the International Court of Justice that Palestinians in Gaza have a “plausible” claim to be protected from acts of genocide.

It would also support trade sanctions on goods linked to illegal settlements in the Occupied Palestinian Territories, back the investigation and prosecution of dual nationals who had fought with the Israel Defence Force and withdrawal of defence and trade officials from Australia’s embassy in Tel Aviv.

Katie Shammas, executive officer at Australia Palestine Advocacy Network (APAN), urged delegates to support Husic’s call.

Israel is committing genocide in Palestine and Labor must help cut off the supply of weapons, investments and political support for these atrocities.

Churches and charities urge stronger federal gambling laws

Josh Butler

A coalition of civil society groups and experts have urged the Albanese government to take stronger action on gambling laws, in a joint submission to the parliamentary inquiry into Labor’s new laws.

The submission - led by the Alliance for Gambling Reform and Wesley Mission - said the government needed to go further with its proposed wagering changes. In the submission, they said:

The Prime Minister [stated] he had three clear goals in relation to these reforms: to break the connection between wagering and sport; to minimise children’s exposure to wagering advertising; and to reduce the saturation of gambling advertising across the internet, radio and TV channels. This Bill does not meet these goals.

Indeed, the groups claimed some of the government’s changes would weaken existing laws, rather than strengthen.

They welcomed the government’s proposals, and the moves to strengthen self-exclusion regulator Betstop, but said “the Bill, as currently drafted, does not go far enough to meaningfully reduce, or indeed prevent gambling harm in Australia. The evidence is clear that stronger, more comprehensive reform is both necessary and achievable.”

Their submission was endorsed by more than 20 more groups, including Anglicare, the Uniting church, ACOSS, DV Connect, and a range of financial counselling, health and suicide prevention organisations.

The top recommendation from the Alliance for Gambling Reform and Wesley was for “a statutory pathway to a full prohibition on all gambling advertising across all platforms - broadcast, digital, email, smart TV’s, venue, and sponsorship - within three years of commencement.”

They also called for a ban on all inducements (such as bonus bets and loyalty incentives) as well as urging the current “opt-out” model for online gambling ads be changed to an “opt-in”. AGR and Wesley said:

Gambling advertising should only be delivered to users who have actively elected to receive it.

Behavioural research consistently shows that most people never change default settings. The burden is placed on individuals — including parents — rather than on government and industry.

Krishani Dhanji

‘To reflect modern Australia’: Labor passes motion to report on diversity in party

Back in Adelaide, Labor delegates have passed a motion to increase multicultural diversity within the party, and to report progress annually on the action.

The motion also includes encouraging each state branch to form multicultural Labor networks to increase the engagement, participation and the election of culturally and linguistically diverse members.

Osmond Chiu speaks on the motion, and says while Labor has made a lot of progress, there’s a long way to go.

[This motion] sets an expectation there will be reporting on diversity of endorsed candidates and commits to invest in the talent pipeline. These changes will help our party better reflect modern Australia.

‘I am shocked’: Former ABC reporter reacts to removal of episodes

Former Four Corners reporter Mahmood Fazal says he is “shocked” by the ABC’s decision to remove two of his episodes amid concerns about the veracity of sources.

Fazal’s employment was terminated by the ABC in May after he appeared on an unauthorised external podcast in 2025, managing director Hugh Marks told Senate estimates.

The ABC announced today it has removed from its digital platforms the Four Corners programs reported by Fazal: Meth Highway (2024) and Cocaine Nation (2023) and associated content.

In a statement posted to social media Fazal said the announcement was “the first I was made aware of by the broadcaster that an investigation into my work was underway.” He said:

The decision to remove these episodes was apparently made before the investigation was completed. I have not been contacted by the Ombudsman, nor have I been told what the apparent issues are.

It is a deeply worrying precedent for the ABC to remove investigative journalism from its flagship programme, apparently in response to what appear to be external criticisms.

Trade minister Don Farrell describes US tariffs on Australia as ‘crazy’

Sarah Basford Canales

Trade minister Don Farrell has described the Trump administration’s decision to impose a 12.5% tariff on Australian exports because Australia is not doing enough to combat forced labour as “crazy”.

Speaking to ABC’s Afternoon Briefing this afternoon from Adelaide, Farrell said it was “absolutely the wrong decision”.

Overwhelmingly, we purchase more goods from the United States than we sell them. You don’t do this to a good trading partner like Australia.

Farrell said a recent discussion with US trade chief, Jamieson Greer, on the topic was “acrimonious” because he did not accept that Australia didn’t have a strong enough system against slave labour. But he did concede it could be improved.

It can be better. We’re trying to improve it, but the idea that the Americans should impose this tariff, an increase in tariff on us for this reason, is just crazy to be honest with you, and the idea that India or Pakistan has a better regime in terms of modern slavery than Australia is simply incorrect.

Read more:

Krishani Dhanji

A low key afternoon at the ALP conference

It’s been fairly quiet this afternoon at the ALP national conference, and like yesterday there have been no fights on the floor (despite previous conferences being well known for their robust debate).

Even the gambling issue earlier was all sorted in the background so when the amendments came up for a vote, there was no one in opposition.

The afternoon’s session has focused on workers’ rights – they’ve supported amendments on paid parental leave which would call for the party to work “with unions and employers on pathways for parents to access 52 weeks paid leave”.

A little earlier, the Australian Council of Trade Unions (ACTU) secretary, Sally McManus spoke to the conference, and welcomed the government’s announcement on AI, warning, “If we do not act, a few billionaires will control our future.”

Next up, the conference will debate on the ALP’s constitution, which will also – no doubt – be pretty low key.

BUT, as my colleague Dan Jervis-Bardy brought you a little earlier, it looks like Labor MP Ed Husic will be bringing some heat to the conference tomorrow, when the party debates a resolution further condemning Israel’s war in Gaza.

Catie McLeod

And with that, I’ll hand over the blog to my colleague Achol Arok, who’ll see you through the rest of the day. Have a good weekend.

Lisa Cox

Government to close Climate Active certification scheme

The Albanese government will scrap a controversial carbon neutral certification program.

Climate Active certified products and businesses that voluntarily purchased offsets as ‘carbon neutral’. More than 100 companies have withdrawn from the scheme in recent years amid concerns about the integrity of carbon offsetting.

The government said on Friday it would close the program but was seeking feedback on two options: simply closing Climate Active, or closing it but retaining some voluntary standards and guidance.

The Australian Conservation Foundation said ending Climate Active was “a good call” and the scheme was “a marketing tool to mislead consumers and investors to buy products that did not yield genuine emissions reduction”.

Climate Council senior advisor Ben McLeod said the scheme “was always a distraction from the real job: cutting climate pollution at the source”.

Jennifer Ansell, chief executive of Arnhem Land Fire Abatement said the voluntary carbon market remained crucial, provided opportunities for remote Indigenous communities, and allowed companies not captured by the safeguard mechanism to “be part of the net zero journey”:

We would like to see something in place so those companies can know they’re achieving those things.

Dan Jervis-Bardy

Ed Husic fighting for Labor to further condemn Israel’s war in Gaza

The Labor MP, Ed Husic, is facing internal resistance as he pushes for the party’s national conference to adopt a resolution further condemning Israel’s war in Gaza.

Guardian Australia understands the outspoken backbencher has drafted a resolution on Israel and Palestine ahead of debate on the party’s foreign policy platform on Saturday morning.

But it was unclear as of Friday afternoon if the resolution would actually be debated.

Sources said factional powerbrokers were attempting to convince left-wing unions not to second Husic’s proposal, meaning it would lapse without reaching the conference floor.

The government - including the foreign minister, Penny Wong - has been working to avoid a messy debate on Israel and Palestine overshadowing the conference.

Jewish groups and Israel’s embassy in Canberra have been publicly putting pressure on the party to water down the draft text, which they claim is not critical enough of Hamas’s role in the Gaza war, while pro-Palestine supporters within Labor are pushing to strengthen the language.

The right faction-aligned shoppies union has reportedly prepared an amendment to resurrect the platform’s call for Hamas to disarm, after it was dropped from the draft text.

Husic was contacted for comment.

australia.title: Donald Trump hits Australian exports to US with new higher trade tariff over claims of ‘forced labour’
australia.snippet: Australia’s trade minister, Don Farrell, says tariff regime is unjustified and inconsistent with free trade agreement with US Follow our ...
australia.content:
Donald Trump has hit Australian exports with new trade tariffs, claiming the country is not doing enough to combat forced labour, but the Albanese government has demanded he remove them immediately.

The United States announced on Friday morning (AEST) that many Australian exports now attract a new 12.5% tariff as part of a broader regime affecting dozens of countries. However the Albanese government says Australia’s three largest export categories – including beef and gold – will avoid the tariff hit.

In a statement, the US trade department said Australia was on a list of 54 economies it deemed as having “failed to impose and effectively enforce a prohibition on the importation of goods produced with forced labor”. Other countries facing a 12.5% tariff include Brazil, China, Egypt, Israel, Japan, New Zealand, Norway, Russia and Singapore.

Economies on a separate list – including the UK, India, Indonesia, Canada and Mexico – will be subject to a lower 10% tariff after the US claimed they had only failed to “enforce” forced labour prohibitions.

Friday’s news followed through on an earlier threat from the Trump administration to level such tariffs, which came after the US supreme court earlier this year struck down Trump’s 10% global tariffs.

Trump had responded to that court ruling by immediately announcing temporary trade sanctions, which were due to expire today.

Australian government sources had previously told Guardian Australia they believed the forced labour-related tariffs had been levelled as a replacement for the tariffs struck down by the courts.

US congresswoman Linda Sánchez, a California Democrat, has denounced the pretext for the new tariffs as a sham.

“President Trump isn’t serious about combating forced labor. He’s trying to make an end-run around the Supreme Court and Congress to reimpose his illegal tariffs,” Sánchez wrote on social media.

The American trade action document claims “the United States is the only country in the world to adopt, and effectively enforce, a ban on imports made with forced labor”.

“President Trump is asking all trading partners to join the United States in eliminating forced labor from global supply chains.”

In total the tariffs apply “to the top 60 U.S. trade partners covering 99.4% of U.S. imports”, according to a trade department statement.

The Australian trade minister, Don Farrell, immediately called for the US to change course.

“These tariffs are unjustified, inconsistent with our free-trade agreement and should be removed,” Farrell said.

“Australia’s measures to combat forced labour and modern slavery are among the strongest in the world and we are recognised globally, including in the US, for our leadership.”

On the ABC’s Afternoon Briefing program, Farrell said has previously had “acrimonious” talks with the US trade chief, Jamieson Greer, over tariffs.

“The idea that the Americans should impose this tariff … is just crazy to be honest with you,” he said.

“And the idea that India or Pakistan has a better regime, in terms of modern slavery, than Australia is simply incorrect.”

The deputy prime minister, Richard Marles, told ABC radio the US actions “make no sense”.

“Forced labour is definitely something which needs to be combated around the world, so we support that objective,” he said. “But we have laws, which are amongst the strongest in the world, and we’ve been making that point to the Trump administration.”

The US trade action document that sets out the new tariffs includes exemptions for a range of goods including beef; agricultural products such as vegetables and fruits; aircraft parts; certain coal, oil, mineral and chemical products; some metal and steel products; timber products; and machinery.

The shadow trade minister, Matt Canavan, claimed the Albanese government had “failed” exporters by not securing lower tariffs, like the UK or Canada.

“Australia is subject to a 12.5% tariff rate, the same rate as Russia, China and Venezuela,” the Nationals’ leader said.

Canavan said the government had “failed to take meaningful action against forced labour in international supply chains, despite years of warnings”.

The Australian Chamber of Commerce and Industry’s chief executive, Andrew McKellar, described the move as a “ludicrous decision” and “completely unjustified”.

The Business Council of Australia’s head, Bran Black, said the US trade chief’s finding rests on a “narrow claim” without “identifying a single company, enforcement failure, or quantified trade impact”.

The National Farmers’ Federation’s chief, Michael Guerin, said the industry was “profoundly disappointed”.

“Rather than moving back towards the free and fair trading arrangements that have served both our countries well for two decades, the United States has chosen to further increase barriers to trade, despite Australia’s longstanding record of high standards and responsible trade,” he said.

The action, as it pertains to Australia specifically, states that after an investigation, “the Trade Representative has determined to impose 12.5 percent tariffs on products of Australia” except for a limited number of exemptions.

australia.title: Afternoon Update: Christian Brothers abuse survivors to be compensated; Trump’s new tariffs; and Alan Turing’s cheeky side
australia.snippet: Want to get this in your inbox every weekday? Sign up for the Afternoon Update here , and start your day with our Morning Mail newsletter...
australia.content:
Good afternoon.

The entity that was gifted vast property holdings by the Christian Brothers has agreed to help compensate abuse survivors in full, in a stunning reversal after weeks of public pressure. The Christian Brothers, a Catholic order with a long history of clergy abuse, last month announced it was going broke and could not afford to meet civil claims from abuse survivors.

In South Australia, conservation groups have questioned why their advertisements targeting Labor politicians were pulled by Adelaide airport for breaking rules on political advertising, while others promoting gas and mining kept running.

And in global news, Donald Trump has hit Australian exports with new trade tariffs, claiming the country is not doing enough to combat forced labour, but the Albanese government has demanded he remove them immediately.

Top news

  • Socceroos star Cristian Volpato allegedly tests positive for cocaine during roadside test

  • TGA warns of potential links between ‘rare but serious’ eye disorder and GLP-1 related drugs

  • Adelaide airport pulls ads from conservation groups but keeps gas and mining ads during ALP conference

  • Barnaby Joyce’s wife Vikki Campion bans 7.30 from farm after dog incident

  • Qantas tests new ultra long-range Airbus in 17,000km direct flight from France to Melbourne

  • Gina Rinehart offers bonuses for Australian swimming medals as funding gap exposed

In pictures

The man previously charged with killing 19-year-old Melbourne woman Isla Bell has failed in his attempt to have the final charge against him relating to her death thrown out. “It’s just so gruelling, and my heart aches,” Bell’s mother said through tears outside court.

What they said …

“I would have said something about Trump.” – Craig Foster

Socceroo turned commentator Craig Foster has been the face of World Cup coverage on SBS for 24 years, though he was absent from this year’s tournament. This week he revealed why he didn’t appear this year.

Full story

Newsroom Edition: An El Niño summer looms – we need to talk about climate change

Political and media attention this week has once again been squarely focused on One Nation’s antics. But while Pauline Hanson had her Euro summer, many of that continent’s biggest cities were enduring their worst heat stress in recorded history.

In Australia, an El Niño summer is not far away and we may be headed for our hottest winter on record.

Jo Tovey speaks with Mike Ticher and assistant climate editor Donna Lu about whether Australia is being too complacent about the changing climate.

Listen to the episode here

Before bed read

When people think of Alan Turing – the father of modern computing – they might imagine he was arrogant, isolated, humourless, tortured.

But Turing’s little-known short story suggests a more accurate way of remembering him would be as “playful, funny, cheeky, literary, and someone who really liked sex,” according to a Cambridge English literature professor.

australia.title: Australian regulator TGA warns of ‘rare but severe’ eye disorder linked to GLP-1 drugs like Ozempic
australia.snippet: TGA says product information for some diabetes and weight loss drugs updated with warning of NAION disorder Follow our Australia news liv...
australia.content:
Australia’s medicines regulator has issued warnings for several type 2 diabetes and obesity-related treatments – including Ozempic and Mounjaro – over the potential to cause a “rare but severe” eye disorder that could lead to blindness.

The Therapeutic Goods Administration’s (TGA) warning came after several GLP-1 RA medicines marketed in Australia as Ozempic, Wegovy and Mounjaro, among other products, were linked to 36 cases of the condition.

The TGA says the eye disorder – non-arteritic anterior ischaemic optic neuropathy (NAION) – may result in permanent visual impairment and “no treatment has been shown to improve visual acuity outcomes” after the condition develops.

Product information documents for Australians have been updated to reflect the new warning, and patients prescribed the drugs are urged to “seek urgent medical attention if they experience sudden vision loss, including partial loss of vision”.

But the TGA does not recommend patients stop treatment without first consulting a doctor, nor has it placed new restrictions on prescriptions.

Prof Helen Danesh-Meyer, from the Royal Australian and New Zealand College of Ophthalmologists, said that NAION is “a very rare condition” that “needs to be put in perspective” to avoid causing alarm.

“Naturally, blindness is something we all fear. It’s one of the greatest concerns that people have,” she said.

“But it’s still a very rare condition, while the other conditions these medications treat are very common, like heart attacks, stroke and kidney disease. If it helps manage and prevent those life-threatening risks, then for that patient it is probably better to continue it.”

The TGA said it first became aware of the link to NAION in 2024 after a study published in a peer-reviewed medical journal raised concerns, and further evidence of the potential links has since “been closely monitored”.

The regulator said it conducted an independent assessment of the potential association between GLP-1 RAs and NAION, but found “available evidence was conflicting” and sought advice from the national advisory committee on medicines on whether the evidence required “additional risk-mitigation measures”.

The committee concluded that the current evidence called for further action, including updated consumer and clinical safety warnings.

The national database of suspected adverse events involving medicines has recorded 36 cases of the eye disorder linked to the drugs. Ozempic and Wegovy accounted for 23 of the cases, with Mounjaro accounting for 10 and Saxenda for three.

No cases were reported in relation to dulaglutide, which is used in the product Trulicity. One of the reported semaglutide cases had a history of previously using dulaglutide.

Danesh-Meyer said the benefits of the medications remain significant.

“This kind of medication has actually revolutionised the management of diabetes as well as obesity,” she said.

“Therefore, we have suggested that doctors [do] not need to hold this medication … from patients unless they have underlying eye conditions.”

Novo Nordisk, the maker of Ozempic, Wegovy and Saxenda, said “patient safety is a top priority” and that it “continuously monitor[s] the safety profile of our medicines” in collaboration with the TGA and other regulators worldwide.

A spokesperson said semaglutide has been studied in “multiple robust clinical development programs with a total exposure from post-marketing use of over 49 million patient years”.

“Considering the totality of evidence from clinical trials, post-marketing reports and observational studies, alongside the generally low incidence rate of NAION, Novo Nordisk believes that the benefit-risk profile of semaglutide remains favorable,” the spokesperson said.

world.title: Two Russian men jailed in Angola for terrorism and spying
world.snippet: The men were convicted over alleged plan to stage coup and organise deadly demonstrations over fuel prices last year Two Russian men have...
world.content:
Two Russian men have been found guilty by an Angolan court of terrorism and spying after being accused of planning a coup and helping to organise deadly demonstrations in the southern African country last year.

Lev Lakshtanov and Igor Ratchin were sentenced to eight and 11 years in jail respectively. They had denied the charges, claiming they were in Angola for cultural and business activities.

From 28-30 July 2025, a minibus taxi strike over fuel price hikes descended into riots and looting, in which 22 people were killed and more than 1,600 arrested according to official figures.

Angola’s security forces were accused of firing live ammunition at protesters; the government said its “progressive” use of force was justified. Human Rights Watch had previously said Angola employed “excessive force” when it used rubber bullets and teargas to break up a peaceful protest against rising fuel prices on 12 July 2025.

Angolan prosecutors said Lakshtanov and Ratchin wanted to influence next year’s presidential elections, including by funding Angola’s largest opposition party, the National Union for the Total Independence of Angola (UNITA), or by forcing a leadership change within the Popular Movement for the Liberation of Angola (MPLA), which has ruled the country since independence from Portugal in 1975.

Prosecutors also claimed the men were linked to Africa Politology, a Russian disinformation and propaganda network that emerged from the Wagner mercenary group.

Africa Politology was taken over by Russia’s Foreign Intelligence Service (SVR) after the death of the Wagner chief Yevgeny Prigozhin in 2023, according to an investigation by media outlets including Forbidden Stories. Wagner was rebranded as Africa Corps and absorbed by Russia’s military.

Angola, whose economy is highly dependent on oil exports, has historically been close with Russia. During the cold war years of Angola’s 1975-2002 civil war, the Soviet Union and Cuba supported the MPLA, while the US and apartheid South Africa backed its opponents, including UNITA. However, Angola’s president, João Lourenço, has improved relations with the US and Europe since taking power in 2017.

In the last decade, Russia has increased its presence in Africa. The Wagner group and then Africa Corps have provided security for the Central African Republic’s president, Faustin-Archange Touadéra, since 2017.

In 2021, Wagner forces arrived in Mali to support the military junta. Africa Corps also backs the military regimes in neighbouring Niger and Burkina Faso. Since 2023, Russian troops have also been deployed in Equatorial Guinea, Libya and Sudan, according to a US Congress report.

Madagascar’s president, Michael Randrianirina, has also boosted ties with Russia since taking power in a coup in October 2025. There are Russians in his presidential guard and a weekly programme about Madagascar-Russia relations was launched earlier this month on national television.

Two Angolans were also tried alongside the Russians. The sports journalist Carlos Tomé received a two-year suspended prison sentence. Francisco de Oliveira, the secretary-general of UNITA’s youth wing, was acquitted.

Prosecutors have appealed against those sentences, according to the Portuguese news agency Lusa. Lakshtanov and Ratchin have also appealed against their sentences, but will remain in detention while the appeal is processed, according to Lusa.

Russia’s embassy in Angola did not immediately respond to a request for comment.

Agence France-Press contributed to this report

world.title: MoD cancels army training in Kenya over powers to prosecute British soldiers
world.snippet: September exercise called off after Kenya raises concerns over funding and jurisdiction for criminal offences The British army has been f...
world.content:
The British army has been forced to cancel training for its troops in Kenya after the Kenyan government refused to ratify a bilateral defence agreement.

While the UK government wanted to renew the existing agreement, Kenyan lawmakers had sought changes to give local authorities greater powers to hold British soldiers accountable for any offences committed in the country.

According to the Kenyan news outlet the Daily Nation, the dispute centres on which cases Kenya will retain primary jurisdiction over, while the amount of money Britain pays Kenya to host the training camp has also been a sticking point.

The chair of the Kenyan national assembly’s defence, intelligence and foreign relations committee, Nelson Koech, said the two governments were “actively engaging to address these outstanding issues”.

As a result of the Kenyan government’s decision, a planned exercise involving the 1st Battalion the Duke of Lancaster’s Regiment, which was due to begin in September, has been cancelled.

A Ministry of Defence spokesperson said: “The UK highly values its relationship with Kenya, which is underpinned by mutual benefit, respect and cooperation. The UK-Kenya Defence Partnership is one of the great strengths of our relationship. Our joint training and operations with the Kenyan Defence Forces are keeping both Kenyan and British people safe.

“It is with regret that the necessary licences required to allow training to take place in Laikipia later this year have not been forthcoming. As a result, the planned training will now be conducted at an alternative location outside Kenya.”

Kenya also benefits from training of its own armed forces at BATUK, the British army base near Nanyuki, and the presence of British troops is valuable for the economy.

The MoD spokesperson added: “We recognise the disappointment this decision will cause for those who would have benefited from the economic activity generated by the exercise.”

They said the UK government remained “committed to our defence partnership with Kenya”, adding that the UK would “continue to engage closely with the Kenyan government to support the resumption of training in-country at the earliest appropriate opportunity”.

However, there has been sustained pressure from Kenyan people opposed to the British army’s continued presence. Last year, a report to the Kenyan parliament into the base alleged human rights violations, environmental destruction and sexual abuse by British soldiers.

The most high-profile case linked to the base is the death of Agnes Wanjiru, in which a British soldier has been charged with murder. Kenya has retained jurisdiction in the case and an extradition hearing is due to take place in November. Robert Purkiss denies the single charge of murder.

Legal proceedings had stalled since Wanjiru’s death in 2012, but advanced under John Healey’s tenure as defence secretary. As shadow defence secretary, he had called on the previous government to do more to progress the case.

Koech said the committee had called for “stronger accountability measures, including jurisdiction over serious offences, enhanced protection for local communities, and implementation of recommendations arising from the BATUK inquiry”.

world.title: Health worker monitored for Ebola in London hospital after working in DRC
world.snippet: UK resident was evacuated from Democratic Republic of the Congo where there is an outbreak of the disease A humanitarian worker is being ...
world.content:
A humanitarian worker is being monitored at a specialist hospital in London after potential exposure to the Ebola virus.

The UK resident was medically evacuated from the Democratic Republic of the Congo (DRC) where the worker had been treating patients with the disease, the UK Health Security Agency (UKHSA) said.

UKHSA said the person was evacuated as a “highly precautionary measure”, adding: “The individual is not currently displaying any symptoms and remains well, but as a precautionary measure they have been evacuated on a flight chartered solely for the evacuation.

“They are now being assessed and monitored in isolation by infectious disease specialists at a London hospital.”

The agency said the incubation period of Ebola ranges from two to 21 days and the individual will be closely monitored and is required to isolate throughout this period.

There are no confirmed cases of Ebola in the UK and the risk to the general public remains low.

Richard Pebody, the director of epidemic and emerging infections at the UKHSA, said: “This individual has been transferred out of an abundance of caution and we’re pleased they remain well.”

Last month, a patient suspected of having the Ebola virus at a Glasgow hospital tested negative.

Precautionary measures were taken after the patient was admitted to the Queen Elizabeth University hospital.

An outbreak of the disease in the Democratic Republic of the Congo and Uganda in May was declared a public health emergency of international concern by the World Health Organization (WHO).

The virus is transmitted to people from wild animals and then spreads in the human population through direct contact with the blood, secretions, organs or other bodily fluids of infected people and with contaminated surfaces and materials such as bedding or clothing.

According to WHO, symptoms can include fever, fatigue, malaise, muscle, pain, headache and sore throat. These are followed by vomiting, diarrhoea, abdominal pain, rash, and symptoms of impaired kidney and liver functions.

world.title: Healthy diet too expensive for one in three people globally, UN report finds
world.snippet: Global hunger declined for the third year in a row in 2025 but experts call for action to bring down costs of fruit, vegetables and dairy...
world.content:
One in three people cannot afford to eat a healthy diet, a new report has found, prompting calls for urgent action on food affordability.

There are 2.69 billion people unable to afford a diverse diet that meets their energy and nutrient needs, and it will take “immense” amounts of work to achieve the global target of zero hunger by 2030, the annual report from five UN agencies warned.

Global hunger declined for a third consecutive year in 2025, with 7.8% of people affected, down from 8.1% in 2024. There were also signs that a prolonged upward trend in Africa was coming to a halt.

However, the proportion of people who cannot afford a healthy diet remains “extremely high”, said Maximo Torero, chief economist of the Food and Agriculture Organization, one of the report’s authors.

The State of Food Security and Nutrition in the World 2026 report calculated the cost of a healthy diet is 4.28 purchasing power parity (PPP) dollars a day. This means that in any given country, a healthy diet costs the amount of local currency with the same buying power that $4.28 has in the US.

“The extreme poverty line is $3PPP per person,” Torero said. “So it’s significantly higher.”

He said government policies had typically focused on subsidising cereals and starchy staples, rather than meat, dairy, fruit and vegetables.

“That means calories, but not a diversity of diet,” he said, highlighting the impact of this on rates of obesity and diseases such as cancer and diabetes.

Figures from the World Health Organization, another of the UN agencies behind the report, show adult obesity rose from 12.1% in 2012 to 16.2% in 2024.

“It’s extremely urgent,” Torero said. “Obesity [among adults] is growing at a very steep level, so we need to now work intensively on trying to minimise those risks and those hidden costs that that substantial increase in obesity will bring.”

He called for investment in infrastructure, research and development. Modelling in the report suggests more efficient supply chains could bring down the costs of meat and dairy as well as fruit and vegetables. New policies to encourage greater consumption of fruit and vegetables could also pay dividends, he suggested, reducing the economic impact of health issues linked to poor diets.

In Africa, 66.6% of the population was unable to afford a healthy diet in 2025, more than double the levels observed in Asia or Latin America and the Caribbean.

Africa is now home to the highest number of hungry people for the first time, with about 309 million, surpassing Asia’s 292 million, the report showed.

The rise is largely driven by higher population growth on the continent, Torero said, with the proportion of the population going hungry actually starting to decrease “for the first time in years”.

“I think this is extremely important, because the numbers are for 2025, where already we have seen a significant reduction in overseas development assistance in the region,” Torero said.

Shipping restrictions in the strait of Hormuz linked to the conflict in the Middle East are likely to hit next year’s figures, he said.

The report is authored by the FAO, WHO, Unicef, the UN World Food Programme and the International Fund for Agricultural Development.

world.title: São Tomé and Príncipe heads to polls in tense presidential election
world.snippet: Incumbent Carlos Vila Nova hopes to defeat his former party and secure second term as independent Voters in São Tomé and Príncipe go to t...
world.content:
Voters in São Tomé and Príncipe go to the polls for a presidential election on Sunday as one of Africa’s least populous countries seeks to burnish its democratic credentials.

According to the National Election Commission, about 142,000 people are registered to vote in the tiny African state’s elections, approximately 15% of whom live in the diaspora.

Since gaining independence from Portugal in 1975, the island country off Africa’s west coast has built a solid reputation for peaceful, competitive elections. But this year’s vote comes amid a tense political atmosphere and a lingering constitutional crisis.

The president, Carlos Vila Nova, is running for a second term as an independent, rather than as the candidate for the ruling Acção Democrática Independente (ADI), whom he represented when he was elected in 2021.

The tensions between Vila Nova and his former party began in January last year when he dismissed the prime minister, Patrice Trovoada. Trovoada’s replacement, the former justice minister Ilza Amado Vaz, resigned after just three days, before the current holder, Américo Ramos, took office.

On Sunday, Vila Nova will be running against four other candidates including the ADI parliamentary leader, Nito D’Abreu. Another former prime minister, Jorge Bom Jesus, attempted to withdraw his independent candidacy, but missed the deadline and remains on the ballot.

The main opposition party, the Movement for the Liberation of São Tomé and Príncipe, is now part of a broad coalition backing the incumbent president, despite being staunch ADI opponents. Meanwhile, an ADI faction led by Ramos is backing D’Abreu. If no candidate receives more than 50% of the vote, the election will go on to a second round.

The businessman Domingos Monteiro, known as “Nino”, who has been president of the São Toméan Football Federation since 2015, was disqualified after the constitutional court ruled he did not meet the eligibility requirements. Monteiro was born on the island, but his parents never became naturalised citizens after moving from Cape Verde where they were born.

“The constitutional court is violating the principle of equal rights … It is time for descendants born in São Tomé and Príncipe to say no to discrimination, to the culture of xenophobia and persecution,” said Monteiro.

For voters, priorities include tackling government corruption, high inflation, severe youth unemployment, chronic fuel shortages, and frequent blackouts. Rivals of Vila Nova are hoping this will keep him from a second term and propel them to the presidency.

Corruption in São Tomé and Príncipe “is the greatest catastrophe the country has experienced in this half-century [of independence”, D’Abreu said at the presidential debate on Tuesday.

The country is seen as a trusted western ally for security and maritime trade in the Gulf of Guinea, one of the world’s biggest maritime piracy hotspots. It also has offshore oil deposits that make a significant contribution to its economy. Observer missions from the European Union, G7+ and the Community of Portuguese Language Countries are on the ground to monitor the polls.
